w1.title: Foundations
w1.subtitle: What %1% is, how risk is priced, and the three numbers everything else hangs on.
w1.intro:
This world covers Part I and the start of Part II of the %1% %2% book: the definition of the discipline, the economics of reliability, and the %3% → %4% → %5% chain. Everything later in the track (alerting, %6%, release policy, capacity) is derived from these ideas, so the checkpoints here are deliberately strict.

> **How to read this world.** Each lesson ends with an *On %7%* section that maps the idea onto services you already know. The boss at the end drops you into a product-launch negotiation where the %8% is the only argument you have.
w1.l1.title: What %1% is
w1.l1.summary: The definition, the 50% rule, and how %1% relates to %2%.
w1.l1.body:
## The one-sentence definition

%2% is **what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team**. %3%'s Ben Treynor Sloss coined the term in 2003. The premise: the people running production should have the skills and the mandate to replace manual work with software.

The historical alternative is the sysadmin model. Developers write features, operators run them, and the two groups have opposite incentives: dev wants change, ops wants stability. Costs grow linearly with traffic because every new service needs more human hands.

%1%

## The rules that make it work

- **The 50% cap.** %4% spend at most half their time on operational work: tickets, %5%, manual actions. The rest is engineering that reduces future operational work. If ops load exceeds 50% for a team, the overflow is redirected back to the product developers, or the developers join the %6% rotation.
- **Hiring.** %7% are software engineers, or people with equivalent skills plus systems expertise (networking, Unix internals). They are expected to get bored doing things by hand and automate them.
- **Shared ownership.** %8% and product development share a service's %9% and an %10% (next lessons). This turns "reliability vs velocity" from a political fight into arithmetic.
- **Blamelessness and data.** Decisions about launches, rollbacks and priorities are made with measured reliability, not opinion.

## Tenets of %11%

The book lists what an %12% team is responsible for: availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response and capacity planning. Every one of these is later given a concrete practice in this track.

## %13% and %14%

%15% is a set of principles: reduce organisational silos, accept failure as normal, implement gradual change, leverage tooling and automation, measure everything. %16% is a concrete implementation of those principles with opinionated specifics (%17%, %18%, the 50% cap, blameless %19%). The workbook's phrasing: *class %20% implements interface %21%*.

> [aws]**On %22%.** The equivalent of "asking a software engineer to run operations" is treating your account as code: infrastructure in %23%, %24% or %25%, changes via pipelines, operational actions as SSM Automation documents or %26% functions rather than console clicks. A team that resolves incidents by clicking in the console is doing ops; a team that turns each incident into a %27% document, then into an EventBridge-triggered automation, is doing %28%.

## Anti-patterns to recognise

- Renaming the ops team "%29%" without changing hiring, the 50% cap or shared %30%.
- %31% as gatekeepers who approve every deploy by hand (that is %32%, not reliability).
- Measuring %33% success by the number of tickets closed.
w1.l1.q0.q: An %1% team reports that operational work consumed 70% of its time last quarter. According to the %2% model, what should happen?
w1.l1.q0.explain: The 50% cap is enforced by pushing excess operational load back to the developers who own the service. Hiring more %1% just scales the ops team linearly, which is the model %2% exists to replace.
w1.l1.q0.c0: The team hires more %1% to absorb the load
w1.l1.q0.c1: The overflow work is redirected to the product development team, which may also join %1%
w1.l1.q0.c2: The team stops doing engineering projects until the backlog clears
w1.l1.q0.c3: The %1% is lowered so fewer pages fire
w1.l1.q1.q: Which of the following are defining characteristics of %1% as opposed to a traditional operations team? Select all that apply.
w1.l1.q1.explain: Manual approval gates and ticket counts are ops-team symptoms. %1% caps ops work, automates, and shares numeric targets with developers.
w1.l1.q1.c0: Operational work is capped at 50% of time
w1.l1.q1.c1: Engineers are hired for software skills and expected to automate
w1.l1.q1.c2: Reliability targets are shared with product development via %1% and %2%
w1.l1.q1.c3: Every production change requires manual %1% approval
w1.l1.q1.c4: Success is measured by the number of tickets resolved
w1.l1.q2.q: How does the %1% workbook describe the relationship between %2% and %3%?
w1.l1.q2.explain: "class %1% implements interface %2%": %3% states the principles, %4% supplies specific practices such as %5%, %6% and blameless %7%.
w1.l1.q2.c0: They are competing methodologies; a company picks one
w1.l1.q2.c2: %1% is a concrete implementation of the %2% principles, with specific opinions
w1.l1.q2.c3: %1% applies to developers, %2% applies to operators
w1.l1.q3.q: True or false: in the %1% model, the cost of running a service is expected to grow roughly linearly with its traffic.
w1.l1.q3.explain: False. That linear growth is the sysadmin model. %1% aims for sublinear growth by automating away the work that would otherwise need more hands.
w1.l2.title: Embracing risk and the cost of nines
w1.l2.summary: Reliability is a product decision with a price; how to measure and pick a target.
w1.l2.body:
## 100% is the wrong target

Beyond a certain point, users cannot tell the difference between your service and the network, phone or Wi-Fi in front of it. Each extra nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more in engineering, redundancy and slowed velocity, and returns almost nothing users notice. The %2% stance: **reliability is a feature with a cost, and the product decides how much to buy.**

Risk is managed, not eliminated. Unreliability is spent deliberately, on launches, experiments, and simpler architectures, rather than leaked accidentally.

## Two ways to measure availability

**Time-based:** availability = uptime ÷ (uptime + downtime). Simple, but a globally distributed service is never fully "down", so the concept blurs.

**Aggregate (request-based):** availability = successful requests ÷ total requests. This works for any system that processes discrete units of work and lets you compute it per region, per customer, or per API method.

%1%

| Target | Downtime per year | Per 30 days | Per day |
|---|---|---|---|
| 99% | 3.65 days | 7.2 h | 14.4 min |
| 99.9% | 8.76 h | 43.2 min | 1.44 min |
| 99.95% | 4.38 h | 21.6 min | 43 s |
| 99.99% | 52.6 min | 4.32 min | 8.6 s |
| 99.999% | 5.26 min | 26 s | 0.86 s |

The formula for the 30-day numbers: 30 × 24 × 60 × (1 − target). Memorise 99.9% ≈ 43 minutes a month; derive the rest by factors of ten.

## Picking a target

Questions from the book for consumer services:
- What level of availability do users expect? (Are they paying? Is there an alternative?)
- Does this service tie directly to revenue?
- Is it free or paid? Are there competitors offering more?
- What happens to user experience if it fails: broken UI, or lost money?

For infrastructure services the trick is to **offer multiple tiers** with different reliability and cost, instead of trying to satisfy the strictest consumer for everyone. The book's example is a storage layer offering low-latency and high-throughput tiers.

## Risk tolerance is asymmetric

Some failures are far worse than the availability number suggests: a 0.01% failure that loses user data, or that hits every request from one large customer, is not "four nines fine". Note the failure *shape* as well as its rate. Later lessons introduce per-customer %3% and data-integrity practices for exactly this reason.

> [aws]**On %4%.** %5% publishes per-service %6% (for example 99.99% for a multi-AZ %7% %8% deployment, 99.99% for %9% %10% per region, 99.999999999% durability for %11% objects). Your service's achievable availability is bounded by the product of its serial dependencies: a single-AZ %12% instance behind a single-AZ database cannot credibly promise 99.99%. Use these numbers as inputs to your target, and remember an %13% %14% credit does not make your users whole.

## Cost, illustrated

Moving a service from 99.9% to 99.99% typically means: multi-AZ everywhere, automated failover that is regularly exercised, %15% deploys with automatic rollback, no human in the response loop for common failures, and a large cut in release frequency risk. If the product cannot articulate the revenue that protects, the extra nine is a bad purchase.
w1.l2.q0.q: A service has a 99.9% availability %1% measured over a 30-day window. How many minutes of complete downtime can it afford in that window?
w1.l2.q1.q: Over the last 30 days a service handled 120,000,000 requests, of which 84,000 failed. What is its request-based availability, as a percentage? (Give at least two decimals.)
w1.l2.q2.q: A product manager asks for 99.999% availability for a free, ad-supported news site. What is the strongest %1% objection?
w1.l2.q2.explain: The marginal nine costs roughly 10× and is invisible behind the user's own connectivity. Every product deserves an %1%, but the target should match what users can perceive and what the business earns.
w1.l2.q2.c0: It is impossible to achieve on %1%
w1.l2.q2.c1: Users cannot distinguish it from lower targets because their own network is less reliable, so the cost buys nothing
w1.l2.q2.c2: Availability cannot be measured beyond four nines
w1.l2.q2.c3: Free services should not have %1% at all
w1.l2.q3.q: Why does the %1% book prefer request-based (aggregate) availability over time-based availability for large services?
w1.l2.q3.explain: Request-based availability is meaningful for partial outages and can be sliced per region, customer or method. It does not ignore partial outages; it captures them precisely.
w1.l2.q3.c0: It always produces a higher number
w1.l2.q3.c1: Globally distributed services are rarely fully down, so "uptime" is ambiguous, while success ÷ total works for any discrete unit of work
w1.l2.q3.c2: Time-based availability is impossible to compute from monitoring data
w1.l2.q4.q: A storage platform serves both a latency-sensitive checkout service and a bulk analytics job. Which approach does the book recommend?
w1.l2.q4.explain: Infrastructure services should expose reliability tiers, so cost tracks the actual need instead of the most demanding client.
w1.l2.q4.c0: Run the platform at the strictest requirement for everyone
w1.l2.q4.c1: Offer tiers with explicitly different reliability and cost, and let consumers choose
w1.l2.q4.c2: Tell the analytics job to build its own storage
w1.l3.title: %1% and %2%
w1.l3.summary: Choosing what to measure, where to measure it, and how to state a target that means something.
w1.l3.body:
## Three terms, three jobs

- **%8% (%9%):** a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the service. Almost always a ratio: **good events ÷ valid events**, expressed as a percentage.
- **%10% (%11%):** a target value or range for an %12% over a window. "99.9% of valid requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30 days."
- **%13% (%14%):** a contract with consequences (credits, penalties) if an %15% is missed. %16% are rarely involved in writing %17%, but they must keep the internal %18% stricter than any external %19%.

%6%

## Choosing %20%

The workbook's rule: pick the few indicators that best describe the **user's experience**, not everything you can measure. Typical menu by service type:

| Service type | %21% that matter |
|---|---|
| Request/response (API, web) | availability (success ratio), latency (fraction under a threshold), quality (degraded responses) |
| Data processing / pipeline | freshness (age of latest output), correctness, coverage, throughput |
| Storage | durability, availability, latency |

Notes on getting this right:
- Define **valid** events. Exclude what the service cannot be blamed for (malformed requests, %22% caused by clients) or your %23% will measure your users.
- **Latency as a ratio, not an average.** "Fraction of requests served under 300 ms" is an %24%; "average latency" is not, because averages hide the tail that users actually feel. Be careful with percentiles too: track %25% and %26% separately, because a slow tail can hide behind a fast median.
- **Fast errors are still errors.** A 500 returned in 2 ms makes latency look great. Compute latency only over successful responses, or count errors as slow.
- Aggregate at the right place. Client-side or load-balancer measurement captures what users see; server-side measurement misses requests that never arrived.

## Where to measure

Options, from closest-to-user to cheapest: synthetic probes and real-user monitoring → load balancer logs and metrics → application metrics → server logs. The book's guidance: prefer the measurement point that reflects user experience, and accept the trade-off in cost and complexity.

## Writing an %27%

A complete %28% statement has: the %29%, the threshold that makes an event "good", the target percentage, and the window.

> 99.95% of valid %30% requests to the checkout API return a non-5xx response within 400 ms, measured at the load balancer, over a rolling 28-day window.

Window choice matters:

%7%

Rolling windows keep the recent past continuously in view; calendar windows match quarterly planning but "reset" abruptly. %31% generally uses rolling windows for alerting and calendar-aligned reporting for business review. Four-week windows avoid the month-length problem.

## Rules of thumb from the book

- Don't pick a target based on current performance; pick it from user needs, then treat the gap as work.
- Keep it simple: few %32%, few %33%.
- Avoid absolutes ("always available", "infinitely scalable").
- Have as few %34% as possible, and defend the ones you have. If nobody would act when an %35% is breached, it is not an %36%.
- Publish a **buffer**: run internal targets tighter than external promises.
- Don't over-achieve. Users will depend on the reliability you actually deliver, so if you consistently beat the %37%, you have lost the freedom to take risk. %38%'s %39% lock service famously injects planned outages to keep dependents honest.

> [aws]**On %40%.** Load-balancer metrics are the natural %41% source for request-driven services: %42% gives %1%, %2% and %3% (with percentile statistics such as %43%). A success-ratio %44% is a %45% metric math expression such as %4%. For latency %46%, avoid %5%; use percentile statistics or, better, define a %47% %48% rule or a log-derived metric that counts requests over the threshold. %49% can define %50% directly on top of these metrics. For pipelines, freshness is the age of the last successful run, easily emitted as a custom metric from the job.

## Common mistakes

- An %51% computed from server-side averages that looks fine while the tail is on fire.
- An %52% on every metric on the dashboard; nobody can defend forty objectives.
- An %53% on an internal component (%54%, queue depth) rather than user-facing behaviour.
- Treating a met %55% as "nothing to do": the freedom to take risk is the whole point.
w1.l3.q0.q: Which of these is a correctly formed %1% according to the workbook definition (good events ÷ valid events)?
w1.l3.q0.explain: An %1% is a ratio of good events to valid events. Averages hide the tail; %2% is an internal cause, not user experience; a raw error count has no denominator.
w1.l3.q0.c0: Average response time of the API over the last hour
w1.l3.q0.c1: Proportion of valid requests served successfully in under 250 ms
w1.l3.q0.c2: %1% utilisation of the fleet stays below 70%
w1.l3.q1.q: A team measures latency %1% across all responses, including errors. Their backend starts throwing fast 500s. What happens to the %2%?
w1.l3.q1.explain: Fast errors pull the latency distribution down. Compute latency over successful responses only, or count errors as slow, so an outage never makes latency look better.
w1.l3.q1.c0: The latency %1% worsens, correctly reflecting the outage
w1.l3.q1.c1: The latency %1% improves, masking the outage
w1.l3.q1.c2: Nothing changes; errors are excluded automatically
w1.l3.q2.q: Which of these belong in a complete %1% statement? Select all that apply.
w1.l3.q2.explain: %1% + good/bad threshold + target + window. Ownership is important but belongs in the error-budget policy, not the %2% statement.
w1.l3.q2.c1: The threshold that defines a "good" event
w1.l3.q3.q: Why does the %1% book warn against consistently over-achieving an %2%?
w1.l3.q3.explain: Delivered reliability becomes the de facto expectation. %1%'s %2% injects planned outages to stop dependents from assuming more than the %3%.
w1.l3.q3.c1: Users come to depend on the delivered reliability, so you lose the freedom to take risks that the %1% was supposed to buy
w1.l3.q4.q: For a request-driven web service on %1%, which measurement point best reflects what users experience while staying cheap to operate?
w1.l3.q4.explain: The load balancer sees every request that reached your edge, including those the application never handled. Server-side logs and resource metrics miss those and measure causes, not symptoms.
w1.l3.q4.c1: Application Load Balancer request, error and percentile latency metrics
w1.l3.q4.c2: Log lines written by the application after it finishes handling a request
w1.l4.title: Error budgets and the %1% policy
w1.l4.summary: Turning the gap between the %1% and perfection into a shared currency.
w1.l4.body:
## The budget

If the %3% is 99.9%, then 0.1% of events are allowed to fail. That 0.1% is the **%4%**. It is not a failure allowance to be hidden; it is a resource to be spent on things that create value and risk: launches, experiments, infrastructure migrations, planned maintenance.

Error budget remaining = allowed bad events − actual bad events (or the time equivalent). Over a 30-day window at 99.9%, the budget is about 43 minutes of full outage, or the equivalent in partial degradation.

%2%

## Why it resolves the dev/ops conflict

Developers want to ship; operators want stability. With an %5%:

- While budget remains, developers can launch as fast as they like. %6% does not veto releases.
- When the budget is exhausted, launches stop (except fixes that improve reliability) until the %7% is back within target.
- Both sides now argue about the same number, and both are incentivised to keep it healthy: developers because they want to keep launching, %8% because it is the job.

The book's phrase: the %9% lets the team **manage risk instead of arguing about it**.

## The %10% policy

The workbook insists the policy is written down, agreed by product, development and %11% leadership, and applied consistently. A typical policy:

1. While budget remains, releases proceed normally.
2. If the budget for the window is exhausted, feature releases freeze until the %12% has been within %13% for a defined period (say, 7 days).
3. If a single incident consumes more than X% of budget, a %14% is mandatory and its action items are prioritised over features.
4. Repeated exhaustion escalates: the development team joins the %15% rotation, or engineers are reassigned to reliability work.
5. The policy states who can grant exceptions and how they are recorded.

Without a policy, the budget is just a chart. With one, it is an executive-backed decision procedure.

## Burn rate

Burn rate is the speed at which budget is consumed relative to the %16%'s own pace. Burn rate 1 means "exactly exhaust the budget at the end of the window". Burn rate 10 means "exhaust it in a tenth of the window": for a 30-day window, in 3 days.

For an availability %17% with allowed error fraction *e*, and an observed error fraction *x* over some period, %18% = *x* ÷ *e*. Example: %19% 99.9% (e = 0.001), current error rate 1.44% → %20% 14.4. This number becomes the basis of the alerting in World 2.

## What to spend the budget on

- Risky launches and A/B experiments.
- Planned maintenance (rebooting, migrations) that is cheaper without full redundancy.
- Relaxing gates: deploying more frequently, with less bake time.
- Intentional outages to test dependent systems' resilience.

> [aws]**On %21%.** %22% %23% %24% expose remaining %25% and burn-rate metrics that you can alarm on and chart. If you build your own, store the %26% target and window as parameters, compute the bad-event count with metric math over the window, and publish %1% as a custom metric. Wire the policy into the pipeline: a %27% manual-approval stage (or a %28% gate) that reads the budget metric and blocks feature deployments when it is negative is the most literal implementation of "launch freeze".

## Pitfalls

- Budget without a policy: nobody stops shipping.
- Policy without executive backing: the first big launch overrides it, and the budget becomes fiction.
- Counting dependency outages against the wrong team; decide up front whether the budget includes them (it usually should, from the user's point of view).
- Measuring the budget over a calendar month and forgetting that a bad first week leaves three weeks of freeze.
w1.l4.q0.q: A service has a 99.95% availability %1% over 30 days. A single incident caused a full outage for 9 minutes. What percentage of the 30-day %2% did that incident consume? (Round to a whole number.)
w1.l4.q1.q: %1% is 99.9% availability. Over the last hour the service returned errors for 0.6% of requests. What is the %2%?
w1.l4.q1.explain: Burn rate = observed error fraction ÷ allowed error fraction = 0.006 ÷ 0.001 = 6.
w1.l4.q2.q: The %1% is exhausted with 12 days left in the window. The product team wants to ship a new feature that does not touch reliability. What does a functioning %2% policy say?
w1.l4.q2.explain: The policy exists precisely for this conversation. Any feature change carries risk; the freeze holds until the service recovers. Changing the %1% to dodge the freeze destroys the policy's credibility.
w1.l4.q2.c0: Ship it, since the feature does not affect reliability
w1.l4.q2.c1: Feature launches freeze until the %1% is back within %2% for the agreed period; only reliability improvements ship
w1.l4.q2.c2: Ship it but double the %1% staffing
w1.l4.q2.c3: Raise the %1% target to make the budget positive again
w1.l4.q3.q: Which of these are legitimate ways to "spend" %1%? Select all that apply.
w1.l4.q3.explain: Budget buys risk-taking that creates value. Skipping learning or falsifying data are not spending; they are cheating.
w1.l4.q3.c0: Running a risky migration with reduced redundancy
w1.l4.q3.c1: Launching an experimental feature to 10% of users
w1.l4.q3.c2: Skipping the %1% for a small incident
w1.l4.q3.c3: Deploying more frequently with shorter %1% bake times
w1.l4.q3.c4: Reporting a lower error count than measured
w1.l4.q4.q: What is the essential ingredient that turns an %1% from a chart into a decision mechanism?
w1.l4.q4.explain: Dashboards and alerts inform; the policy decides. Without leadership agreement, the first important launch overrides the freeze and the budget loses meaning.
w1.l4.q4.c1: A written policy agreed by product, development and %1% leadership, with consequences and exception rules
w1.l4.q4.c2: An automated alert on the budget
w1.l5.title: Toil
w1.l5.summary: What %1% is, why it is corrosive, and how to measure and eliminate it.
w1.l5.body:
## Definition

Toil is not simply "work I don't enjoy". The book gives it a precise shape. Toil is operational work tied to running a production service that is:

- **Manual** – a human runs it, even if it is just running a script by hand.
- **Repetitive** – done over and over; not a novel problem.
- **Automatable** – a machine could do it as well as a human, if you built the machine.
- **Tactical** – interrupt-driven and reactive rather than strategy-driven.
- **Devoid of enduring value** – the service is in the same state after the work as before.
- **O(n) with service growth** – scales linearly with users, traffic or size.

Work that meets several of these is %1%. Overhead (meetings, reviews, HR paperwork) is not %2%; it is not tied to running the service. Engineering work that permanently improves the service is the opposite of %3%.

## Why it matters

%4% targets **less than 50%** of each %5%'s time on %6%. The reasons are practical: %7% crowds out the engineering that reduces future %8%, it does not scale, it burns people out, it slows the team's career growth, and it sets a bad precedent (other teams will hand you their %9% too).

A little %10% is fine; some people even find predictable, low-risk tasks calming. The problem is when it dominates.

## Where %11% comes from

Typical sources: manual releases, hand-applied config changes, quota and capacity requests, restarting things, rotating credentials by hand, responding to alerts that need no judgement, onboarding new tenants by copying a template, "please run this query for me".

## Measuring it

The workbook recommends tracking %12% explicitly: survey the team, tag tickets, or sample time. Rank sources by hours per month × frequency, and pick the largest that is cheapest to automate. Ask for each: could the system detect the condition itself? Could it fix it itself? Could the requester self-serve?

## Eliminating it

Tactics in rough order of leverage:
1. **Remove the need** – change the design so the task never occurs (e.g. autoscaling instead of manual capacity adds).
2. **Self-service** – hand the task to the requester with guardrails (a form, an API, a pull request).
3. **Automate fully** – the system detects and acts (auto-remediation).
4. **Automate partially** – a one-command tool a human triggers; still %13%, but faster and safer.
5. **Batch and schedule** – if it must be manual, do it in bulk at planned times, not on interrupt.

> [aws]**On %14%.** The canonical %15% toil-killers: %16% groups instead of manual instance adds; %17% Automation %18% triggered by %19% alarms or %20% rules for auto-remediation; %21% rotation instead of hand-rotated credentials; %22% or account-vending automation for self-service provisioning; %23% %24% rules with remediation actions for drift. A useful test: if an %25% engineer has run the same SSM document by hand three times, the fourth run should be an %26% target.

## The trap

Automating %27% is engineering work, so it competes with feature requests and rarely feels urgent. That is why the 50% cap is a rule and not a suggestion: it forces the trade-off to be made explicitly, with data, instead of by whoever shouts loudest.
w1.l5.q0.q: Which of the following activities count as %1% under the %2% book's definition? Select all that apply.
w1.l5.q0.explain: Manual, repetitive, automatable, no enduring value: capacity adds, alert-driven restarts and hand-onboarding are %1%. Designing autoscaling is engineering; planning meetings are overhead.
w1.l5.q0.c0: Manually adding %1% capacity every Monday ahead of the weekly traffic peak
w1.l5.q0.c1: Designing an autoscaling policy so capacity adds happen automatically
w1.l5.q0.c2: Restarting a stuck worker process in response to the same alert, twice a week
w1.l5.q0.c4: Approving each new tenant by hand-editing a config file and deploying it
w1.l5.q1.q: What is the ceiling %1% sets for the fraction of an %2%'s time spent on %3%?
w1.l5.q1.explain: The 50% cap applies to all operational work, of which %1% is the largest component. Consistently exceeding it triggers redistribution of work to the development team.
w1.l5.q2.q: Which elimination tactic has the highest leverage according to the ordering in this lesson?
w1.l5.q2.explain: Removing the need beats self-service, which beats full automation, which beats partial automation. Reassigning %1% does not reduce it.
w1.l5.q2.c0: Write a script the %1% engineer runs on demand
w1.l5.q2.c1: Change the design so the task no longer needs to happen
w1.l5.q2.c2: Batch the manual task into a weekly session
w1.l5.q2.c3: Assign the task to a junior engineer
w1.l5.q3.q: True or false: work that is unpleasant but requires genuine engineering judgement each time (for example, debugging a novel performance regression) is %1%.
w1.l5.q3.explain: False. Toil is repetitive and automatable. Novel, judgement-heavy work is engineering, however unpleasant.
w1.boss.title: The Launch Dilemma
w1.boss.tagline: Product wants to ship. The budget says otherwise. You have the numbers; use them.
w1.boss.intro:
You are the %1% for **Checkout**, a payment API on %2% (%3% → %4% → %5%). The %6%: 99.9% of valid requests succeed within 500 ms, rolling 30 days. The error-budget policy is signed by the VP of Engineering.

It is day 22 of the window. Two incidents this month (a bad deploy, and an %7% failover that took longer than expected) consumed **81%** of the budget. Product wants to launch "One-Click Reorder" on day 24, ahead of a marketing campaign.

Your service-health meter tracks both reliability and the credibility of the %8% function. Keep it above 50% to clear the world.
w1.boss.win:
Checkout finished the window inside its %1% with budget to spare, two features shipped, and the policy held without becoming a weapon. The key moves: refusing to make the budget negotiable, fixing the dependency design before launch, spending budget in canary-sized pieces, and treating latency as a first-class %2% component.

**Takeaway:** the %3% only works when %4% says *yes, and here is how* at least as often as it says *not yet*.
w1.boss.lose:
Checkout breached its %1%, or the %2% function lost the credibility it needs to enforce the policy next time. Common failure paths in this scenario: excluding incidents from the budget on request, letting a serial 99.5% dependency into a 99.9% path without a fallback, rolling a known latency regression forward, or over-freezing while budget remained.

Re-read lessons 1.3 and 1.4, then retry.
w1.boss.s0.text:
The product lead opens with: "We've been at 99.9% or better the whole month except for two blips. Those were %1% issues, not ours. Why should our launch pay for them?"

Current numbers: budget remaining 19%, %2% over the last 7 days 0.4×.
w1.boss.s0.c0.text: Explain that the budget is shared and blameless by design: whose fault the incidents were is irrelevant to how much risk the service can absorb now. Show the 19% and the policy.
w1.boss.s0.c0.fb: Correct framing. The budget measures the service's remaining tolerance for risk from the user's point of view; attribution belongs in the %1%, not in the launch decision.
w1.boss.s0.c1.text: Concede the point since the incidents were infrastructure-related, and agree to exclude them from the budget calculation.
w1.boss.s0.c1.fb: You just made the budget negotiable. Once exclusions are granted case by case, the policy no longer constrains anyone.
w1.boss.s0.c2.text: Refuse the launch flatly and end the meeting.
w1.boss.s0.c2.fb: The budget is not exhausted. A flat refusal is not what the policy says, and it costs you credibility for the day the policy does require a freeze.
w1.boss.s1.text:
You look at the launch plan. The feature adds a new dependency: a call to a recommendations service (owned by another team) inside the checkout request path, with a 2-second timeout and no fallback. Its %1% is 99.5%.

What is your first concern?
w1.boss.s1.c0.text: A 99.5% dependency in the serial request path caps Checkout below its own 99.9% %1%; the design needs a fallback and a much shorter timeout so recommendation failures do not become checkout failures.
w1.boss.s1.c0.fb: Exactly. Serial dependencies multiply. With a fallback (skip recommendations) and a tight timeout, the dependency degrades quality instead of availability.
w1.boss.s1.c1.text: The 2-second timeout is fine because the %1% idle timeout is 60 seconds.
w1.boss.s1.c1.fb: A 2-second stall inside a 500 ms latency %1% turns every recommendations slowdown into an %2% violation. The %3% timeout is irrelevant.
w1.boss.s1.c2.text: Ask the recommendations team to raise their %1% to 99.9%.
w1.boss.s1.c2.fb: That is a months-long conversation; it does not fix this launch. Design the caller to tolerate the dependency you actually have.
w1.boss.s2.text:
The dev team implements a 150 ms timeout with a fallback that skips recommendations. Product now asks: "So can we launch to 100% on day 24?"

Budget remaining: 19%. Projected campaign traffic: +40%.
w1.boss.s2.c0.text: Yes, but as a progressive rollout: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% over 48 hours, each stage gated on the %1%, with automatic rollback. The remaining budget can absorb a %2% failure; it cannot absorb a full-fleet failure.
w1.boss.s2.c0.fb: This is spending the budget deliberately. A 1% %1% that fails costs a sliver of budget; a 100% failure would exhaust it within minutes.
w1.boss.s2.c1.text: Yes, to 100%, since there is budget left.
w1.boss.s2.c1.fb: Nineteen percent of budget is about 8 minutes of full outage. A bad full-fleet deploy would blow through it before the rollback finished.
w1.boss.s2.c2.text: No. Wait until the window rolls over on day 30.
w1.boss.s2.c2.fb: Overly conservative: the policy does not require a freeze while budget remains, and a rolling window does not "reset" on day 30 anyway.
w1.boss.s3.text: Canary at 10%. %1% shows %2% latency on %3% tasks at 620 ms vs 310 ms on baseline; error rate unchanged. The marketing email goes out in two hours.
w1.boss.s3.c0.text: Halt the rollout at 10% and roll the %1% back. The latency %2% is part of the %3%; a doubled %4% at 10% would breach it at 100%.
w1.boss.s3.c0.fb: Right call. Latency violations count against the same budget as errors. Investigate (the fallback path is probably not the only thing that changed), fix, re-canary.
w1.boss.s3.c1.text: Proceed to 50% because the error rate is fine.
w1.boss.s3.c1.fb: The %1% includes a 500 ms threshold. You just scaled a known %2% violation to half the fleet, two hours before a traffic spike.
w1.boss.s3.c2.text: Hold at 10% and wait for the marketing spike to see if it gets worse.
w1.boss.s3.c2.fb: Holding a known-bad %1% in front of 10% of users during a campaign is spending budget for no information you did not already have.
w1.boss.s4.text:
Root cause: the new code path made an extra synchronous %1% query per request. Fixed, re-canaried, rolled out to 100% successfully. Budget remaining: 15%.

Product now proposes a second launch, "Gift Wrapping", on day 27. It is a small UI change with no backend impact.
w1.boss.s4.c0.text: Agree, with the standard progressive rollout. Fifteen percent of budget is enough to absorb a canary-scale failure, and a UI-only change is low risk. Note it in the launch log.
w1.boss.s4.c0.fb: Consistent with the policy: budget remains, risk is proportionate, and the launch is recorded. This is what "%1% does not veto releases" looks like in practice.
w1.boss.s4.c1.text: Refuse: the budget is too low for any launch.
w1.boss.s4.c1.fb: The policy freezes launches at zero budget, not at 15%. Inventing a stricter threshold on the spot is as corrosive as ignoring the policy.
w1.boss.s4.c2.text: Agree, and skip the %1% because it is UI-only.
w1.boss.s4.c2.fb: "No backend impact" is what every UI change says until it triples an API call count. The %1% is cheap; the budget is not.
w1.boss.s5.text: Gift Wrapping shipped without incident. The %1% for the day-24 latency regression is drafted. The dev lead asks to skip the review meeting because "we already fixed it".
w1.boss.s5.c0.text: Hold the review. The fix addressed the symptom; the action items (a load test in the pipeline that catches added DB queries per request, and a latency gate in the %1% analysis) are what stop the next one.
w1.boss.s5.c0.fb: The %1%'s value is in the action items and the shared learning, not in the fix. Review it, assign owners, track completion.
w1.boss.s5.c1.text: Skip the review; the fix is in.
w1.boss.s5.c1.fb: You just traded the only durable output of the incident for an hour. The same class of regression returns next quarter.
w1.boss.s5.c2.text: Hold the review, and identify who wrote the extra query so it does not happen again.
w1.boss.s5.c2.fb: Blame ends the flow of honest information. The next engineer who spots a risky change will stay quiet.
